transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-16
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 48m
Attendees: Eli Navarro, Priya Shah, Jordan Li (Redwood) — Maya Chen, Owen Park, Lara Gomez, Samir Rao (NorthStar)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): NorthStar is evaluating a migration path from OpenAI API and internal TGI/vLLM hosts to Redwood. Focus on parity testing, security, and clear cost/sla tradeoffs. They have regulatory customers requiring auditability.

[00:00] Eli Navarro: hey everyone thanks for joining, we just wanted to kick off, uh, a quick discovery to understand what you're running today and what success looks like.
[00:18] Maya Chen: thanks eli, yep, i'll do a quick overview. we're currently on OpenAI for most user-facing generation, and we have an internal stack that uses TGI and v L M for some heavy-batch reranking and offline scoring. the reason we're talking to you is twofold: we're looking to lower unit cost for high-volume inferencing and also explore private deployments for a set of regulated financial customers.
[00:36] Owen Park: (adds) infra-wise we run kubernetes, we have a mix of A100s on prem and some GCP instances. for the TGI stuff it's mostly internal, we use the community TGI container and a vllm fronting layer.
[00:50] Priya Shah: got it, thanks. when you say "vllm fronting layer" — are you seeing the usual kv cache warmups and latency spikes with long context?
[00:58] Owen Park: yes, the kv cache behaviour is a pain, warm starts take time, and tail latency under burst is our biggest issue. also cost math on OpenAI has been creeping up as we push more tokens.
[01:12] Jordan Li: quick clarifying q — what models on OpenAI are you using? gpt-4o? gpt-4o-mini?
[01:18] Maya Chen: mostly gpt-4o for chat and some 4o-mini for lower-cost endpoints. but keep in mind we've tuned prompts and postprocess to reduce hallucinations for our domain.
[01:26] Eli Navarro: perfect, and what are your success criteria — what would make a migration successful for you?
[01:31] Maya Chen: three things: 1) parity on quality for our eval set (we have ~1,200 seed prompts with graded labels), 2) <100ms p95 for our synchronous endpoints in Dedicated mode, and 3) security controls — SSO, KMS, audit logs, retention policies.
[01:46] Lara Gomez: and for compliance we need exportable audit trails + proof of encryption at rest keys that we control, ideally HSM/KMS integration.
[01:55] Priya Shah: good, that's in line with what we see. Redwood has both Hosted and Dedicated and a Private option where you control the KMS. we can plug into your KMS via standard customer-key wrapping or HSM depending on requirement. we'll send the integration notes.
[02:10] Maya Chen: two questions on parity — a) will Redwood run models exactly as you do in TGI? and b) what about tokenizer differences / sampling seeds? we care about determinism for some regressions.
[02:22] Priya Shah: great q. so Redwood's runtime is tuned for production and we support the models you're likely running; however, some differences in kernel numerics and quantization can cause small deltas. for parity testing we usually do a side-by-side run with the same tokenizer and seed where possible and measure n-gram overlap, instruction-following metrics, and domain accuracy. we also capture token-level logs for debugging.
[02:47] Owen Park: and about the TGI container — will you take existing weights as-is? our team has custom builds and a small adapter layer.
[02:54] Eli Navarro: in many cases yes, we can ingest model artifacts compatible with the model family; if you're running custom ops we might need to recompile or use a compatible variant. sometimes it's easier to bring a quantized copy. we'll note that as part of the POC scope.
[03:10] Samir Rao: pricing — what's the delta between Hosted and Dedicated? we're doing roughly 10M tokens a month across several endpoints.
[03:18] Eli Navarro: high-level — Hosted is pure usage pricing; Dedicated is reserved capacity and is typically cheaper at scale once you commit. we'll send a worksheet with committed vs burst options. Dedicated also gives you more control over latency because you get reserved GPU pools.
[03:34] Maya Chen: on latency targets we need p95 <100ms for the chat path. is that realistic on Hosted?
[03:40] Priya Shah: Hosted can hit low latencies in some regions, but Dedicated or Private with pinned GPUs is the safer path for strict p95 targets — because you avoid noisy neighbor and have deterministic batching. also, caching (prefix/KV cache) reduces per-token compute when warm.
[03:58] Lara Gomez: about audit logs, retention — can we export logs to our SIEM? we have strict retention policies for 7 years for some customers.
[04:06] Jordan Li: yes, we support log export to S3 and SIEM integrations, and retention policy controls in the console; for long-term retention we typically set up an archival flow to your cloud bucket. we'll share a sample network diagram.
[04:20] Maya Chen: okay, great. i'm also worried about model regression — we've seen prompts that were tuned for OpenAI behave differently on other runtimes. how often do you see regressions when porting from OpenAI?
[04:31] Priya Shah: regressions do happen, usually for safety-sensitive prompts or where sampling behavior differs. our Optimize toolkit helps by running continuous evals against your seed set and raising alerts on regression. for the POC we recommend a small canary rollout and side-by-side A/B testing for a week.
[04:50] Owen Park: operational question — does Redwood manage autoscaling or do we? we want to control scaling policies for cost reasons.
[04:57] Eli Navarro: Dedicated provides autoscaling policies you can configure; for Private you manage scaling via your infra team but we provide the control plane. we'll review autoscale hook options in the deep-dive.
[05:08] Samir Rao: any customers in fintech or regulated finance you can point to? references matter for our compliance folks.
[05:14] Jordan Li: yes, we have a couple of regulated customers; we'll include anonymized references and an enterprise reference call if you'd like.
[05:22] Maya Chen: perfect. on the technical side for the parity run — what artifacts do you need from us?
[05:27] Priya Shah: ideally: 1) canonical eval prompt set (seeds and labels), 2) a small representative traffic trace (latency/seq length distribution), 3) the model artifact or model spec (if you have a custom TGI container, let us know), and 4) a prioritized list of endpoints.
[05:45] Maya Chen: we can pull that together — we'll scrub PII where needed.
[05:50] Lara Gomez: SSO — we use Okta. do you support SAML/SCIM and fine-grained RBAC?
[05:56] Jordan Li: yes, we support SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC roles at project and token level. audit trails tie into token usage in the Console.
[06:06] Owen Park: a nit — we're using mixed hardware and a subset of on-prem. how does Private on-prem actually work? is the control plane still hosted?
[06:14] Eli Navarro: the Private offering has a customer-managed data plane; the control plane can be in a private VPC or hosted depending on contract. you can opt for fully air-gapped in extreme cases. for KMS you can provide keys via your KMS.
[06:28] Priya Shah: quick note on quantization — if you use lower-bit quantized models in TGI you might see different quality. part of the parity run is testing the quantization profile.
[06:38] Maya Chen: okay, for our POC can you replicate our TGI inference path including the same batching logic? we want apples-to-apples.
[06:45] Priya Shah: we'll try to replicate batching and sampling where possible; sometimes exact replication requires instrumenting the runtime. we'll log tokens and sampling metrics so you can compare.
[06:57] Samir Rao: what's the usual timeline for a POC? this is for a board review late May so we need results before then.
[07:04] Eli Navarro: a typical POC is 2–4 weeks: week 0 discovery and setup, week 1 parity runs, week 2 load tests and integration checks, then a findings deck. to hit late-May board review, we should start next week.
[07:17] Maya Chen: sounds tight but possible.

[07:30] (Discussion: specific prompts)
[07:30] Maya Chen: one example — we have a regulatory summarization prompt that is sensitive to hallucinations; we hack prompts and a custom post-filter. we'll include it in the eval set.
[07:40] Priya Shah: we can run the same prompt and also run our reranker to compare factuality scores. often the differences show up in prefix handling and tokenization edge cases.
[07:52] Owen Park: are there any known issues moving from OpenAI's API semantics to your runtime? e.g., function calling differences or streaming semantics?
[07:59] Priya Shah: we support function/tool calling and streaming; semantics are generally equivalent but some naming and error codes differ. we provide a shim layer in the client lib to make migration easier.
[08:12] Lara Gomez: data residency — we have EU customers. can we pin region?
[08:16] Jordan Li: yes, you can pin region for Hosted, and Dedicated/Private obviously give you more control. we'll provide region-specific deployment notes.

[08:30] (brief silence, note-taking)

[08:40] Eli Navarro: quick recap before we go deeper: items to share — SOC2/security pack, pricing worksheet, POC scope. we'll also run an initial parity test on your seed prompts.
[08:51] Maya Chen: great. two follow-ups: a) will the parity run be run on your Hosted infra or Dedicated test pool? and b) can we get raw token-level logs to debug?
[09:00] Priya Shah: the initial parity will be on a dedicated test pool (not shared production) to control variables; yes, we'll provide token-level logs with redaction options.
[09:10] Owen Park: any showstoppers around licensing for the model artifacts? we have a mix of open weights and some licensed variants.
[09:17] Eli Navarro: licensing varies — open weights are fine; for licensed or vendor-proprietary artifacts we'd need to check the TOU. if you have vendor restrictions we'll work through legal.

[09:30] (Customer asks about benchmarks)
[09:30] Samir Rao: can you run a cost/latency sim for our workload? sequence lengths vary — average 1,200 tokens on some flows.
[09:39] Priya Shah: yes, provide traffic distribution and we'll run a simulated batch run to estimate per-token cost with and without KV caching. we'll include recommended quantization profiles to meet cost targets.

[09:52] Lara Gomez: any required network ports for Private? we use restrictive egress rules.
[09:57] Jordan Li: we'll send a minimal network diagram. usually it's TLS outbound to a control endpoint and a few ports for the runtime; for air-gapped deployments we can work with your infra team.

[10:08] Maya Chen: one more: regression monitoring — does Redwood hook into our CI for continuous evals?
[10:14] Priya Shah: yes, our Optimize tool can be integrated into your CI/CD; you can push evals and get regression alerts.

[10:25] (Recap / Close)
[10:25] Eli Navarro: ok next steps — we'll: share security pack (Jordan), send pricing worksheet (Eli), SE parity run (Priya). we'll propose a technical deep-dive slot week of 2026-04-27.
[10:40] Maya Chen: that works. thanks everyone, we'll deliver the eval prompts and traffic profile by 4/21.
[10:46] Eli Navarro: awesome, thanks all.

(End meeting)
